Performance outcome

The rider turns track knowledge into a race-run plan, separates practice goals from race goals, chooses where to commit and where to be conservative, and reviews the run afterwards with their coach.

Who it’s for

Competitive downhill and enduro riders.

Before this lesson

  • Race Track Walk.
  • Practice Laps, Section Splits and Video Analysis.

Why it matters

Race runs are scored on one attempt. Consistency and good decisions under pressure often matter more than the fastest possible line.

Technical model

Source check: d01 (video only: not yet watched). The reviewer must confirm this section against the original.

Practice laps and race runs have different jobs

Practice is for testing and learning; the race run is for executing the plan. Mixing the two leads to untested changes on race day.

The cost of an error

A small time gain from a risky line can be wiped out by one mistake. Riders decide in advance where to commit and where to ride conservatively.

Routines

A consistent warm-up and pre-run routine helps riders arrive at the start ready. This lesson stays at a general performance level; it isn’t sports psychology or medical advice.

Debrief

After the run, the rider reflects first and then reviews with the coach: what went to plan, what didn’t, and why.

Physics & maths

Expected time

Expected value helps compare lines: if a risky line saves a little time when it works but costs a lot when it doesn’t, multiply each outcome by its likelihood and add them up. A line that is slower but almost never goes wrong can have the better expected time.

A good Mathlete visual: an expected-value calculator for two lines, using the rider’s own practice data.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection

Practice design

Setting
Race simulations on a known track, under coach supervision.
Focus
Execute a written plan; review against it.
Feedback
Run plan, video, splits, rider reflection and coach debrief.

Stop when

  • Fatigue.
  • Conditions change.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Did the rider follow the plan?
  • Where were errors made and what did they cost?
  • Consistency across simulated race runs.
  • Quality of the rider’s reflection.

Ready to move on

  • The rider writes a run plan, executes it in a simulation and debriefs it with the coach.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
